---
title: "Exercise 2 - A probability that disappears"
output: github_document
---

```{r setup}
x <- c(5, 8, 10, 20, 30, 40)
```

## Compute the upper-tail probability in three different ways

```{r upper tail}
# Upper-tail probability in three different ways
# via complement
p1 <- 1 - pnorm(x)
# direct
p2 <- pnorm(x, lower.tail = FALSE)
# log-scale
lp <- pnorm(x, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE) 

# Collect the three results in a data frame
print(data.frame(x, p1, p2, lp), digits = 5)
```

## Identify where the first expression begins to give a misleading answer

In this section we analyse the first expression, which computes the upper tail as $1 - P(Z \le x)$.

As a reference we use p2.

```{r analysis-of-p1}
# Determine relative error
rel_err <- abs(p1 - p2) / p2
# Collect the results in a data frame
print(data.frame(x, p1, p2, rel_err), digits = 5)

x[which(rel_err > 0.05)[1]]
x[which(p1 == 0)[1]]
```

`p1` and `p2` still agrees at x = 5. At x = 8 it is off by about 7%, and from x = 10 on it returns exactly 0.

## Explain why `1 - pnorm(x)` can fail even when `pnorm(x)` itself is accurately computed

Subtracting two nearly equal numbers is where precision is lost. This destroys the accuracy that `pnorm(x)` has. 

`pnorm(x, lower.tail = FALSE)` avoids this because it computes the tail directly, with no subtraction, so the relative accuracy is preserved.

## Why `1 - pnorm(x)` can fail even when `pnorm(x)` is accurate

Doubles carry about 16 significant digits, so every stored number has a relative rounding error of about $10^{-16}$. For relatively large $x$, `pnorm(x)` is very close to 1 and doubles near 1 are spaced only about $1.1 \cdot 10^{-16}$ apart. `pnorm(x)` is therefore computed with a small relative error, but it carries an absolute error of that size, and the tiny upper tail $P(Z > x)$ is the part of the number that falls below this spacing.

The subtraction $1 - \Phi(x)$ then removes the leading digits, which are all equal to 1, and what remains is mostly rounding error. This is cancellation: the absolute error stays the same, while the result is much smaller, so its relative error becomes large. At $x = 8$ the true tail is $6.2 \cdot 10^{-16}$, only a few units of the spacing, and `1 - pnorm(8)` returns $6.66 \cdot 10^{-16} = 6 \cdot 1.11 \cdot 10^{-16}$, about 7% too large. Once the tail is below the spacing, `pnorm(x)` rounds to exactly 1 and the result is 0, as for $x \ge 10$.

`pnorm(x, lower.tail = FALSE)` avoids the problem because it computes the tail directly, without subtracting from 1, so the relative accuracy is kept.
